Glendalough
glen-duh-LOKH
n. (the Wicklow valley monastery founded by Kevin, a see united to Dublin in 1214)
Irish Gleann Dá Loch, the glen of two lakes, from gleann, a glen, and loch, a lake.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Glendalough is a deep glen in the Wicklow mountains with two lakes in it, where Kevin, or Coemgen, settled as a hermit in the late sixth century and found a community growing round him whether he wanted one or not. The monastery that resulted filled the lower valley with churches, a round tower, a gatehouse and a cathedral, and became a diocese; it was repeatedly burned by Norsemen and by the Irish, and in 1214 the see was united with Dublin, after which the valley declined into a pilgrimage resort with a reputation for riotous gatherings on Kevin's day that the archbishops eventually suppressed. The dictionary records Glendalough for the honest tension in its founder's life, which the hagiographers exaggerated into legend but did not invent: a man goes apart to pray and is given people to teach. Christ commands the closet and the shut door for prayer, and Paul says he wants men free to attend on the Lord without distraction; neither text makes solitude an end, and both assume a man who comes back out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a closet as a small private apartment for retirement; secret as hidden and concealed; a distraction as a drawing apart of the mind; to continue as to persevere; and to faint as to lose courage.

expand to see more

CLOSET, n. A small room or apartment for retirement; any room for privacy; a private repository of curiosities.

SECRET, a. Separate; hid; concealed from the notice or knowledge of all persons except the individual concerned.

DISTRACTION, n. A drawing apart; separation; a drawing of the mind in different directions; perturbation of mind.

CONTINUE, v.i. To remain in a state, or place; to abide for any time indefinitely; to persevere; to be steadfast.

FAINT, v.i. To lose the animal functions; to lose courage or spirit; to sink into dejection; to grow weak.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:6 — "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly."

1Co 7:35 — "And this I speak for your own profit; not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for that which is comely, and that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction."

Luk 18:1 — "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;"

Col 4:2 — "Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;"

Modern Corruption

Wicklow valley monastery founded by Kevin, grown from a hermitage into a diocese, united to Dublin in 1214 and later a riotous pilgrimage resort.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the shut door is commanded and the shut life is not. Christ gives the command with its reason and its reward: “enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). Paul wants the same freedom from interruption for the single believer, and he says plainly why, “that ye may attend upon the Lord without distraction” (1Co 7:35), which is an aim and not a vocation of hiding.

The two live temptations at Glendalough are both documented in its own history. One is the pilgrimage that turned a hermit's glen into a fair with drink and fighting in it, which the archbishops of Dublin had to put down. The other is to treat withdrawal as the whole of devotion rather than as the room in which devotion is practised. Christ's parable on prayer gives the real discipline, “that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1), and Paul puts it as a standing order to ordinary congregations: “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2). Kevin got a community; he kept the hours.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek tameion (G5009), an inner chamber; Greek kruptos (G2927), hidden; Greek aperispastos (G0563), without distraction; Greek proskartereo (G4342), to persevere.

expand to see more

Greek tameion (G5009) — an inner chamber, a storeroom; “enter into thy closet”, Matthew 6:6.

Greek kruptos (G2927) — hidden, secret; “pray to thy Father which is in secret”, Matthew 6:6.

Greek aperispastos (G0563) — without distraction, undividedly; “attend upon the Lord without distraction”, 1 Corinthians 7:35.

Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to faint; “and not to faint”, Luke 18:1.

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to continue steadfastly; “Continue in prayer”, Colossians 4:2.

Usage

"“when thou hast shut thy door” (Mat 6:6) — the room, commanded."

"“attend upon the Lord without distraction” (1Co 7:35) — the aim, not the hiding."

"“that men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1) — the real discipline."
